title: Minimum Right Shifts to Sort the Array
statement:
You get an array `nums` of `n` distinct positive integers. One right shift moves every element one place to the right at the same time, and the last element wraps around to index `0` (the value at index `i` goes to index `(i + 1) % n`).

Return the smallest number of right shifts after which `nums` is in increasing order, or `-1` if no number of right shifts can sort it.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Shifting right only rotates the array, so the sorted result has to start with the smallest value. That pins down where the rotation must begin: at the index of the minimum. Instead of trying every shift count (the brute force, O(n²)), simulate reading the array once from that index, wrapping around the end, and check that each value is larger than the one before.

## Approach

1. Scan `nums` and keep `start`, the index of the smallest value.
2. Walk `step` from `1` to `n - 1`, reading `previous` and `current` at positions `start + step - 1` and `start + step`, both taken modulo `n`.
3. If any `previous` is larger than `current`, the circular order is broken and no rotation sorts the array: return `-1`.
4. Otherwise the value at `start` must travel to index `0`, which takes `(n - start) % n` right shifts.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]`, `n = 5`. The minimum `1` sits at `start = 3`. Reading from there gives `1, 2, 3, 4, 5` (indices 3, 4, 0, 1, 2), and every pair increases. The answer is `(5 - 3) % 5 = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass to find the minimum and one circular pass to check the order.
- Space: O(1): only a few indices are stored.

## Pitfalls

- An already sorted array has `start = 0` and needs `0` shifts, not `n`; the `% n` handles that.
- Checking only that there is one "drop" inside the array is not enough: the last value must also be smaller than the first, which the wrap-around read catches (`[2, 1, 4]` fails here).
- A right shift moves values to higher indices, so the count is `n - start`, not `start`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `start` | index of the smallest value, where the sorted order must begin |
| `step` | how far the circular read has advanced from `start` |
| `previous`, `current` | two neighbouring values in the circular read |

narration.2: Remember the length; every index in the circular read is taken modulo n.
narration.3: Assume the smallest value is at index 0 until a smaller one shows up.
narration.4: Scan the rest of the array for the minimum.
narration.5: A smaller value means the sorted order would have to begin here instead.
narration.6: Record its index as the new start.
narration.9: Read the array circularly from start, one neighbouring pair at a time.
narration.10: The value just before this position in the circular read.
narration.11: The value at this position, wrapping past the end with % n.
narration.12: A decrease anywhere means no rotation can sort the array.
narration.13: Report that sorting by right shifts is impossible.
narration.16: Every pair increased, so moving start to index 0 takes (n - start) % n right shifts.
